scope: 70 further original AS Physics and Chemistry short flashcards eligible for school mocks, balanced across circuits, measurement, graphs, waves, materials, nuclear physics, Amount of Substance, energetics, atomic structure, bonding, Group 7, kinetics and organic recall. No Maths Year 2 or untaught Physics A2.

previouslyFalseFullCreditExamples.wrong: A superconductor has a large resistivity below its critical temperature.
Its resistivity only falls to zero above the critical temperature.
The vertical intercept is always zero for a cell with emf.
Strangeness is always conserved by weak interactions and violated by strong interactions.
The wave frequency doubles whenever the wave enters a denser medium.
Divide the salt moles by water moles to find x.
x equals mass of water divided by mass of hydrated sample without converting to moles.
The enthalpy sign stays unchanged when the reaction is reversed.
Cr: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; Cu: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.
Remove the 3d electrons before any 4s electron.
Always remove electrons from 3d and 4s alternately.
Group 1 makes +2 ions, group 2 makes +1 and group 13 makes +3.
Group 15 ions are −1, group 16 ions are −2 and group 17 ions are −3.
The arrow points from the electron-pair acceptor towards the donor.
Chloride loses an electron more readily than iodide and is the stronger reducing agent.
Primary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than tertiary.
Bromine water changes from colourless to orange after adding an alkene.
Small alcohols are soluble because they cannot hydrogen bond with water.
Structural isomers necessarily have different molecular formulae.

method: Each selected card is an unchanged existing one-fact core flashcard. Add one vetted correct paraphrase and two known incorrect distractors keyed to original ID/front/back, then test the actual production evaluator before fuzzy word-overlap scoring.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is an ideal voltmeter's resistance?
rows.originalBack: Infinite.
accept: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
reject: Zero ohms.
An ideal voltmeter has no resistance so it draws maximum current.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why is a diode's current very small in reverse bias?
rows.originalBack: It strongly resists current in the reverse direction.
accept: A reverse-biased diode has very high resistance so almost no current flows.
reject: A reverse-biased diode conducts current freely.
Its reverse resistance becomes zero when it is reverse-biased.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is an NTC thermistor?
rows.originalBack: A component whose resistance falls as temperature rises.
accept: An NTC thermistor has lower resistance at higher temperatures.
reject: Its resistance increases when it gets hotter.
A negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor always has zero resistance.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is a superconductor?
rows.originalBack: A material with zero resistivity below its critical temperature.
accept: Below its critical temperature a superconductor has zero electrical resistivity.
reject: A superconductor has a large resistivity below its critical temperature.
Its resistivity only falls to zero above the critical temperature.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the potential-divider output depend on?
rows.originalBack: The proportion of the total resistance across the output.
accept: The output voltage depends on the fraction of the total divider resistance that is across the output.
reject: The output is independent of the ratio of the two resistances.
Both resistances always receive equal potential differences even when unequal.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the intercept of a V–I graph for a cell?
rows.originalBack: The emf.
accept: The vertical-axis intercept of a terminal potential difference versus current graph is the emf.
reject: It is the cell's internal resistance.
The vertical intercept is always zero for a cell with emf.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the magnitude of a cell's V–I gradient?
rows.originalBack: Its internal resistance.
accept: The magnitude of the negative gradient of terminal V against I is internal resistance r.
reject: The gradient magnitude gives the emf.
The gradient has magnitude equal to reciprocal internal resistance.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How is current shared at a junction?
rows.originalBack: Total current entering equals total current leaving.
accept: Kirchhoff's first law: total current entering a junction equals total leaving.
reject: The total current out of a junction must exceed the current entering.
Electric charge is not conserved at a current junction.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is a random measurement error?
rows.originalBack: An unpredictable variation causing scatter in repeated measurements.
accept: Random errors cause scatter or unpredictable fluctuations between repeated readings.
reject: They make every reading too large by the same fixed amount.
Random errors shift all measurements by exactly the same offset.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: When calculating uncertainty in a quantity proportional to d², how does percentage uncertainty in d contribute?
rows.originalBack: Its percentage uncertainty is doubled for the squared factor.
accept: The squared diameter contributes twice the percentage uncertainty in diameter.
reject: Halve the diameter's percentage uncertainty when squaring.
Percentage uncertainty in d squared is the same as in d.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Convert 1 cm² into m².
rows.originalBack: 1 cm² = (10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m².
accept: 1 cm squared equals 10 to the minus 4 square metres.
reject: 1 cm² equals 10⁻² m².
1 cm² is 10⁴ m².

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Convert 1 electronvolt (eV) into joules.
accept: 1 eV is approximately 1.60 times 10 to the minus 19 joules.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Convert 1 kilowatt-hour into joules.
accept: One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 million joules.
reject: 1 kWh equals 3600 J.
1 kWh is 3.60 × 10⁹ joules.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the difference between a horizontal line on s–t and v–t graphs?
rows.originalBack: s–t horizontal: v = 0 (stationary). v–t horizontal: a = 0 (constant velocity).
accept: A flat displacement–time graph shows zero velocity; a flat velocity–time graph shows zero acceleration.
reject: A horizontal s–t graph shows constant nonzero speed and a horizontal v–t graph shows a stationary object.
On a horizontal v–t line acceleration must be positive.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A velocity–time graph encloses +15 m and −21 m of area. Find displacement and total distance.
rows.originalBack: Displacement = 15−21 = −6 m. Distance = 15+21 = 36 m.
accept: Displacement is minus 6 metres, whereas total distance travelled is 36 metres.
reject: Displacement is 36 m and total distance is −6 m.
Displacement and total distance are both 6 m.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: On an s–t graph the gradient is negative but becomes less steep. Is the object speeding up?
rows.originalBack: No. Velocity is negative but its magnitude decreases, so the object slows down.
accept: No, the magnitude of its negative gradient decreases, so it slows down.
reject: Yes, a negative slope that is becoming shallower always means speeding up.
The object is accelerating in the negative direction and increasing its speed.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: On an s–t graph, what does a steeper negative gradient mean?
rows.originalBack: Greater speed in the negative direction.
accept: A steeper negative displacement–time gradient indicates a larger speed towards the negative direction.
reject: A steeper negative gradient means the object must move in the positive direction.
The negative velocity has smaller magnitude as the line gets steeper.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the elastic limit?
rows.originalBack: Beyond it, unloading leaves permanent deformation.
accept: Beyond the elastic limit, the sample does not fully recover its shape on unloading.
reject: The elastic limit is precisely where force is no longer proportional to extension.
Past the elastic limit the sample returns exactly to its original length when unloaded.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the limit of proportionality?
rows.originalBack: Point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to force.
accept: Beyond the limit of proportionality, force and extension are no longer linearly proportional.
reject: The limit of proportionality is necessarily the point where the sample breaks.
Force and extension stay proportional beyond the proportional limit.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does the area under a force–extension graph represent?
rows.originalBack: Work done in stretching the material.
accept: The area beneath force plotted against extension equals the mechanical work done stretching the sample.
reject: The area always gives the spring constant.
The area under F–extension is equal to the force divided by extension.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What changes in a nucleus during alpha decay?
rows.originalBack: Nucleon number −4; proton number −2.
accept: Alpha emission decreases mass number by four and proton number by two.
reject: Alpha decay reduces mass number by two and proton number by four.
The mass number is unchanged in alpha decay.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What changes in a nucleus during beta-minus decay?
rows.originalBack: Proton number increases by 1; nucleon number stays the same.
accept: In beta-minus decay the proton number rises by one while mass number stays unchanged.
reject: The proton number falls by one while nucleon number is unchanged.
Beta-minus emission reduces nucleon number by one.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to the strong nuclear force at extremely small separations?
rows.originalBack: It becomes repulsive.
accept: At extremely short distances, the strong nuclear force becomes repulsive.
reject: The strong nuclear force is always attractive, even at arbitrarily small separations.
At very small separations the strong interaction disappears entirely.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which bosons carry the weak interaction at A-level?
rows.originalBack: W⁺ and W⁻ bosons.
accept: Weak interactions are mediated by W+ and W− bosons in the A-level treatment.
reject: Only photons carry the weak interaction.
Gluons carry the weak decay interaction instead of W bosons.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What quantity is conserved in strong but not always weak interactions?
rows.originalBack: Strangeness.
accept: Strangeness is conserved in strong interactions, but can change in weak interactions.
reject: Strangeness is always conserved by weak interactions and violated by strong interactions.
Electric charge is not conserved by strong interactions.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What happens to wave speed when frequency doubles in the same medium?
rows.originalBack: It stays the same.
accept: Wave speed stays constant in the same medium when the frequency doubles; wavelength halves.
reject: Wave speed doubles when frequency doubles in the unchanged medium.
Doubling frequency halves the wave speed in the same material.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Which wave property is fixed by its source across a boundary?
rows.originalBack: Frequency.
accept: The source fixes frequency, which remains unchanged when crossing into another medium.
reject: Wavelength stays the same across the boundary even when speed changes.
The wave frequency doubles whenever the wave enters a denser medium.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the distance between adjacent stationary-wave nodes?
rows.originalBack: Half a wavelength.
accept: Successive stationary-wave nodes are separated by lambda divided by two.
reject: Adjacent nodes are separated by one full wavelength.
A node and the next node are a quarter of a wavelength apart.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is the phase relation of particles between adjacent nodes?
rows.originalBack: They oscillate in phase.
accept: Points in one stationary-wave loop between neighbouring nodes vibrate in phase.
reject: Points between adjacent nodes vibrate 180 degrees out of phase.
Every point in a stationary wave is always in phase with every other point.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Fill the gap: a stationary-wave node has ____ amplitude.
rows.originalBack: A point of zero amplitude.
accept: At a stationary-wave node the amplitude is zero.
reject: The node has the maximum amplitude.
A node oscillates with the same nonzero amplitude as the antinode.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is percentage yield?
rows.originalBack: actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
accept: Actual product yield divided by theoretical maximum product yield, multiplied by 100.
reject: Theoretical yield divided by actual yield, multiplied by 100.
Percentage yield equals actual yield divided by total reactant mass without mole calculations.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is percentage purity calculated?
rows.originalBack: mass of pure substance ÷ total sample mass × 100.
accept: Mass of desired pure substance divided by whole sample mass multiplied by 100.
reject: Mass of impurities divided by sample mass multiplied by 100.
Total sample mass divided by pure substance mass multiplied by 100.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: For salt·xH₂O, how is x found from the amounts in moles?
rows.originalBack: x = moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt.
accept: Find the mole ratio of water lost to moles of anhydrous salt; this is x.
reject: Divide the salt moles by water moles to find x.
x equals mass of water divided by mass of hydrated sample without converting to moles.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Can a reaction have high atom economy but low percentage yield?
rows.originalBack: Yes. Theoretical atom use can be efficient even if little product is recovered.
accept: Yes, efficient theoretical atom use can coexist with a poor isolated reaction yield.
reject: No, high atom economy guarantees a high actual percentage yield.
Atom economy and experimental percentage yield must always be numerically identical.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Define standard enthalpy of formation precisely.
rows.originalBack: ΔH when 1 mol of compound forms from elements in standard states under standard conditions.
accept: Formation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from elements in their standard states.
reject: The enthalpy change on making two moles of the substance from any reactants.
The enthalpy change of decomposing one mole of the compound into gaseous atoms.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Is ΔfH° of gaseous oxygen atoms O(g) zero?
rows.originalBack: No; oxygen's standard state is O₂(g).
accept: No; elemental oxygen has standard state O₂(g), not atomic O(g).
reject: Yes, all elemental oxygen species have zero standard formation enthalpy.
Yes, oxygen atoms in the gas phase are the standard state of oxygen.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What happens to ΔH if a whole reaction equation is doubled?
rows.originalBack: ΔH for the doubled equation also doubles.
accept: The enthalpy change doubles if every reaction coefficient is multiplied by two.
reject: Doubling every reaction coefficient halves the reaction enthalpy.
Doubling the balanced equation leaves the reaction enthalpy unchanged.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What happens to ΔH if a reaction is reversed?
rows.originalBack: The enthalpy sign reverses.
accept: The reverse reaction has the opposite sign of enthalpy change but the same magnitude.
reject: The enthalpy sign stays unchanged when the reaction is reversed.
Reversing a reaction forces the enthalpy change to become zero.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why is 2H₂(g)+O₂(g)→2H₂O(l) not a one-mole formation equation?
rows.originalBack: It forms 2 mol H₂O; halve every coefficient for standard molar formation.
accept: The equation makes two moles of water so divide every stoichiometric coefficient by two for a one-mole formation equation.
reject: This equation forms one mole of water and is already a standard formation equation.
Double each coefficient again to write a one-mole formation equation.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What are the exceptional electron configurations of chromium and copper?
rows.originalBack: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Cu: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹.
accept: Chromium is [Ar]3d5 4s1, whereas copper is [Ar]3d10 4s1.
reject: Cr: [Ar]3d⁴4s²; Cu: [Ar]3d⁹4s².
Cr: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; Cu: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the configuration of Fe²⁺?
rows.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁶; electrons are removed from 4s before 3d.
accept: An iron(II) ion has [Ar]3d6 with both 4s electrons removed.
reject: Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁴4s².
Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the configuration of Fe³⁺?
rows.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁵; after both 4s electrons, one 3d electron is lost.
accept: Fe3+ is [Ar]3d5 because both 4s electrons and one 3d electron are lost.
reject: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d³4s².
Fe³⁺ has the configuration [Ar]3d⁶.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: When transition-metal ions form, which electrons leave first?
rows.originalBack: The 4s electrons are removed before 3d electrons.
accept: When forming transition-metal cations the 4s electrons are removed before the 3d electrons.
reject: Remove the 3d electrons before any 4s electron.
Always remove electrons from 3d and 4s alternately.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What charges do Group 1, 2 and 13 elements commonly form?
rows.originalBack: +1, +2 and +3 ions respectively.
accept: The common charges are group 1 +1, group 2 +2 and group 13 +3.
reject: Group 1 makes +2 ions, group 2 makes +1 and group 13 makes +3.
Common Group 1, 2 and 13 metal charges are all negative.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What charges do Group 15, 16 and 17 non-metals commonly form?
rows.originalBack: −3, −2 and −1 ions respectively.
accept: The common ion charges are 15 −3, 16 −2 and 17 −1.
reject: Group 15 ions are −1, group 16 ions are −2 and group 17 ions are −3.
Each of these non-metals usually forms positive ions with charges +3 +2 +1.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
rows.originalBack: (NH₄)₂CO₃: two NH₄⁺ balance one CO₃²⁻.
accept: (NH4)2CO3, because two singly positive ammonium ions balance one carbonate 2− ion.
reject: NH₄CO₃.
(NH₄)₃CO₃.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is a coordinate bond represented in a diagram?
rows.originalBack: With an arrow pointing from electron-pair donor to acceptor.
accept: A dative bond arrow goes from the electron-pair donor towards the electron-pair acceptor.
reject: The arrow points from the electron-pair acceptor towards the donor.
The arrow has no relationship to which atom supplies the shared electron pair.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why can a metal carry electrical current in the solid state?
rows.originalBack: Mobile delocalised electrons carry charge through the lattice.
accept: Mobile delocalised electrons move through the lattice and carry current.
reject: Solid metals conduct because positive metal ions move freely through the solid.
Metals contain mobile protons responsible for electrical conduction.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How does halogen electronegativity change down Group 7?
rows.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: Electronegativity generally decreases down Group 7.
reject: Halogen electronegativity increases down Group 7.
Electronegativity stays identical from fluorine down to iodine.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How do halogen boiling points change down Group 7?
rows.originalBack: They increase.
accept: Boiling points of Group 7 halogens increase down the group.
reject: Halogen boiling temperatures become lower down Group 7.
Fluorine has the highest boiling point in the group.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is disproportionation of chlorine in cold alkaline solution?
rows.originalBack: Cl₂ forms chloride and chlorate(I) ions.
accept: Chlorine disproportionates to chloride and chlorate(I) in cold dilute alkali.
reject: Cold dilute alkali produces chloride and chlorate(V) as the main products.
Chlorine is only reduced and never oxidised during this disproportionation.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why are iodide ions better reducing agents than chloride ions?
rows.originalBack: Iodide loses an electron more easily.
accept: Iodide is oxidised more readily because it gives up an electron more easily than chloride.
reject: Chloride loses an electron more readily than iodide and is the stronger reducing agent.
Iodide is a better reducing agent because it gains electrons more easily.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How does increasing temperature change the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve?
rows.originalBack: It broadens, lowers its peak and shifts to higher energies.
accept: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution flattens and broadens, with its peak at greater energy on heating.
reject: The curve becomes taller and narrower with its maximum shifting to lower energies.
The area under a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution must double whenever temperature doubles.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does the area under a Maxwell–Boltzmann curve represent?
rows.originalBack: Total number of molecules in the sample.
accept: The area beneath the energy distribution is the total number of particles in the sample.
reject: Area under the curve measures only particles with energy above activation energy.
The total area represents the temperature of the gas.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does the gradient of a concentration–time graph represent?
rows.originalBack: Instantaneous rate of concentration change.
accept: The tangent gradient gives instantaneous concentration change per unit time; its sign depends on the species.
reject: The concentration-time gradient gives the total amount of product ever made.
A concentration–time graph's gradient is always positive even for a reactant being consumed.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is activation energy?
rows.originalBack: Minimum energy required for a successful collision.
accept: The minimum energy required for a successful collision.
reject: Activation energy is the maximum energy the reactants can have.
Activation energy is the energy released when new bonds form.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Order typical carbocations by stability.
rows.originalBack: Tertiary is more stable than secondary, which is more stable than primary.
accept: The stability order is tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary carbocation.
reject: Primary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than tertiary.
Primary, secondary and tertiary carbocations have the same stability.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What colour change indicates an alkene with bromine water?
rows.originalBack: Orange to colourless.
accept: Bromine water changes from orange to colourless when it reacts with an alkene.
reject: Bromine water changes from colourless to orange after adding an alkene.
Bromine water stays orange when it undergoes the usual alkene addition reaction.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What condition permits E/Z isomerism around a C=C bond?
rows.originalBack: Each double-bond carbon has two different groups.
accept: Each C atom of the double bond must carry two different attached groups.
reject: Both carbons on the double bond must each have two identical attached groups.
A free-rotating single bond on its own is the requirement for E/Z isomerism.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does E mean in E/Z stereoisomerism?
rows.originalBack: Higher-priority groups are on opposite sides.
accept: For E stereoisomers the highest-priority groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.
reject: E means that highest-priority groups lie on the same side of the double bond.
E requires a carbon-carbon single bond that rotates freely.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does Z mean in E/Z stereoisomerism?
rows.originalBack: Higher-priority groups are on the same side.
accept: For Z stereoisomers the higher-priority groups are on the same side of C=C.
reject: Z means that the highest-priority substituents are opposite one another.
Z signifies no restriction on rotation at the C=C bond.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does further oxidation of a primary alcohol produce?
rows.originalBack: A carboxylic acid.
accept: Further oxidation of a primary alcohol gives a carboxylic acid.
reject: Extended oxidation of a primary alcohol produces a ketone.
An oxidised primary alcohol can only give a secondary alcohol.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does oxidation of a secondary alcohol produce?
rows.originalBack: A ketone.
accept: Oxidising a secondary alcohol normally produces a ketone.
reject: A secondary alcohol oxidises to an aldehyde.
Secondary alcohols oxidise directly to a carboxylic acid under normal dichromate conditions.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What forms when an alcohol undergoes dehydration?
rows.originalBack: An alkene and water.
accept: Dehydration removes water from an alcohol to form an alkene.
reject: Dehydration adds water to the alcohol to produce a carboxylic acid.
A hydrated alcohol gives an alkane and hydrogen as its dehydration products.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What happens when alcohols react with sodium?
rows.originalBack: An alkoxide and hydrogen form.
accept: Reaction of an alcohol with sodium produces a sodium alkoxide and hydrogen.
reject: Sodium reacts with an alcohol to release oxygen gas and form a carboxylate.
Alcohol plus sodium produces a ketone and water.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why are small alcohols soluble in water?
rows.originalBack: They form hydrogen bonds with water.
accept: Small alcohol molecules can hydrogen-bond to water molecules.
reject: Small alcohols are soluble because they cannot hydrogen bond with water.
Their solubility is due solely to ionic bonds forming between hydrocarbon chains.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Where should the tail of a curly arrow be placed?
rows.originalBack: At an electron pair: a lone pair or covalent bond.
accept: The curly arrow starts from a lone pair or covalent bond that supplies the electron pair.
reject: Start a full curly arrow at an atom with no electrons to donate.
The tail is placed on the electron-pair acceptor rather than on an electron pair.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is a structural isomer?
rows.originalBack: Same molecular formula, different structural formula.
accept: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
reject: Structural isomers necessarily have different molecular formulae.
Structural isomers differ only in their three-dimensional arrangement with identical connectivity.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is chain isomerism?
rows.originalBack: Same molecular formula but a different carbon skeleton.
accept: Chain isomers share a molecular formula but differ in their carbon skeleton.
reject: Chain isomerism means moving the same functional group on an unchanged carbon skeleton.
Chain isomers must have different molecular formulae.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does 'displayed formula' show?
rows.originalBack: Every atom and every covalent bond.
accept: A displayed formula depicts each atom and every bond between them.
reject: A displayed formula shows just the carbon skeleton without any other atoms.
Displayed formulae never show individual covalent bonds.
